overview: This file contains a covering letter and an attached memorandum from Irving Pflaum of the Coordinator of Information’s Foreign Information Service urging federal action to restrict American press publicity for Japanese radio broadcasts naming U.S. prisoners of war. Pflaum argues that reporting derived from Tokyo broadcasts advertises an enemy propaganda outlet and assists Japanese psychological warfare, even if the broadcasts themselves appear ineffective. He recommends asking news organizations and private monitoring services to suppress references to the programs while having a U.S. government agency promptly release the prisoners’ names, allowing newspapers to continue local human-interest coverage without directing readers to enemy radio.

subfiles.title: Letter from Irving Pflaum to James Dunn transmitting memorandum on Japanese broadcasts
subfiles.from: Irving Pflaum, Chief, News Division, Foreign Information Service
subfiles.about: Pflaum transmits a memorandum circulated to the Committee on War Information and urges action against publicity for Japanese broadcasts.
subfiles.summary: Pflaum informs Dunn that all members of the Committee on War Information are receiving the attached memorandum so that they will understand the problem posed by Japanese broadcasts. He expresses concern that American publicity is gratuitously strengthening an enemy propaganda instrument and hopes that corrective action will be taken. The page also bears State Department filing and receipt annotations.

subfiles.title: Memorandum to Robert Sherwood on censorship of Japanese prisoner broadcasts
subfiles.about: Pflaum argues for suppressing press references to Japanese prisoner broadcasts while replacing enemy-radio monitoring reports with official U.S. releases of prisoners’ names.
subfiles.summary: Pflaum describes the memorandum as his office’s third or fourth attempt to resolve the problem of American publicity for Tokyo radio broadcasts naming captured servicemen. He contends that such publicity gives aid to Japanese psychological warfare by attracting listeners and creating opportunities for rumors, dissension, and division, warning against repeating the underestimation of Japan associated with Pearl Harbor. He proposes that Byron Price ask press associations, independent newspapers, and private listening posts to withhold information about the broadcasts. The War Department, Federal Communications Commission, or another agency would instead release the reported names with an error warning, permitting newspapers to pursue local stories without advertising Japanese radio; copies were also sent to Price, Lowell Mellett, and other members of the Committee on War Information.

interest: The file provides a compact view of early-1942 debates over how a democracy should manage enemy propaganda without eliminating legitimate news about captured servicemen. Particularly useful is Pflaum’s proposed information-substitution strategy: suppress the enemy source while rapidly reproducing its newsworthy content through official channels. His invocation of Pearl Harbor also shows how recent military surprise was used to argue that Japanese psychological capabilities must not be underestimated, while the reference to repeated prior attempts suggests unresolved bureaucratic disagreement over censorship authority.
